summary:
What it does. Our system identifies, quantifies, and ranks 100 micro-sites on Earth, each a 1 km² operational footprint, as analogs for Moon and Mars targets. Sites span key archetypes: lava tubes (Pisgah), basaltic flows and calderas (Craters of the Moon, Askja), hyper-arid evaporite basins (Salar de Uyuni, Atacama), and permafrost and polar craters (Haughton, Antarctica). We also include vegetated “anti-analog” control sites to confirm the algorithm rejects comfortable Earth environments.

Unified schema. Earth, Moon, and Mars are described in three CSV files that share 19 core columns (terrain, lithology, thermal behavior, ice, dust, albedo), plus planet-specific engineering filters.

Zero-download data pipeline. We send coordinates to cloud services: NASA POWER, Open-Elevation, Macrostrat, Copernicus/Google Earth Engine (Sentinel-2/3, SAR), and NASA PDS/Orbital Data Explorer (LRO Diviner/LOLA, MGS MOLA, Odyssey THEMIS).
Matching. k-Nearest Neighbors finds the closest Earth analogs across the 19 shared features. TOPSIS then ranks sites between a positive ideal (extreme space-like conditions) and a negative ideal (vegetated controls).
Impact. The pipeline is lightweight, reproducible, and extensible, giving mission planners a transparent, data-driven shortlist of test sites for habitats, rovers, drilling, and ice harvesting.
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

The Multi-Planet Terrestrial Analog Matching Engine is a cloud-native geospatial and machine learning pipeline that finds the places on Earth that best resemble landing zones and outposts on the Moon and Mars.

Rather than comparing broad regions, we focus on 100 micro-sites on Earth, each a 1 km² operational footprint. They cover the geological settings space missions care about most: lava tubes (Pisgah), basaltic flows and calderas (Askja), hyper-arid salt flats (Salar de Uyuni), permafrost and polar craters (Haughton), and acidic, iron-rich terrain (Rio Tinto). We also added vegetated “anti-analog” control sites, which the engine should reject.

We built the dataset without downloading any large satellite rasters. Instead, we send each site’s coordinates to cloud services and retrieve only the values we need:

  • NASA POWER provides surface temperature (mean, min, max), precipitation, wind speed, and albedo.
  • Open-Elevation is queried on a 3×3 grid of points about 55 m apart around each site, from which we compute elevation, slope, and terrain roughness in memory.
  • Macrostrat provides bedrock lithology and geologic units.
  • Copernicus openEO and Google Earth Engine provide Sentinel-2 vegetation cover (NDVI), Sentinel-3 ice and snow fraction, and SAR backscatter.
  • NASA PDS and the Orbital Data Explorer provide lunar data (LRO Diviner, LOLA) and Martian data (MGS MOLA, Odyssey THEMIS), served from pre-binned grids indexed with a scipy cKDTree for fast lookups.

All results are organized into three aligned files (earth.csv, moon.csv, mars.csv) that share 19 core columns, including elevation, slope, roughness, thermal inertia, albedo, temperature range, and ice indicators. Each file also has planet-specific engineering fields.

For matching, k-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) measures distance across the shared features to find the closest Earth sites to a given lunar or Martian target. TOPSIS then ranks candidates between a positive ideal (extreme, space-like conditions) and a negative ideal (vegetated control sites).

2. What benefits does it have?
  • Speed and simplicity. Lightweight point queries replace heavy raster downloads, so there are no local storage bottlenecks and the pipeline can be rerun quickly.
  • Objective site selection. Multi-attribute similarity scoring replaces qualitative “best guess” choices of test sites.
  • Targeted testing. Engineers can match a site to the specific subsystem they are testing, such as rover wheels on rough volcanic basalt or drill bits in frozen ground.
3. What is the intended impact of the project?

As NASA’s Artemis program and future Mars missions move forward, testing hardware and habitats on Earth is essential. Our engine gives planetary scientists, mission planners, and robotics engineers an open, automated way to find the 1 km² site on Earth that best reproduces the terrain, thermal behavior, and mineralogy of a target such as Shackleton Rim on the Moon or Jezero Crater on Mars.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?
  • Language and environment: Python 3 in Google Colab and JupyterLab
  • Libraries: pandas, NumPy, SciPy (cKDTree), requests, scikit-learn
  • Data services: NASA POWER, Open-Elevation, Macrostrat, Google Earth Engine, Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem (openEO/STAC), NASA PDS Search API, and PDS Geosciences Orbital Data Explorer
5. How is your project creative?
  • Inverted GIS workflow. Instead of storing huge rasters, we stream point queries from multiple cloud servers and keep only the exact values needed.
  • Terrain from a tiny sample. Sampling a 3×3 grid around each site lets us compute slope and roughness on the fly, with no GIS software required.
  • Anti-analog controls. Including temperate, vegetated sites as deliberate negative examples lets us check that the ranking pushes comfortable Earth environments toward the bottom.
6. What factors did your team consider?
  • Scale. We kept 1 km² operational footprints separate from regional climate, since landing and outpost work depends on local terrain.
  • Cross-planet comparability. A common 19-feature core lets Earth, Moon, and Mars sites be compared directly in the same feature space.
  • Where analogs break down. Planet-specific variables, such as atmospheric pressure, solar illumination, and permafrost, serve as hard filters so users can see where an Earth site stops being a valid stand-in.
